context: The canto opens with an outburst from the poet before he has described anything. Simon's followers are the simoniacs: churchmen who bought and sold holy offices.

note: The things of God, church offices and sacraments, should be given like brides to good men. The simoniacs sell them instead. The image of the Church as a bride sold or dishonored runs through the whole canto.
A town crier sounded a trumpet before reading out a criminal's sentence. Dante takes the crier's part. Many readers also hear the trumpet of the Last Judgment.
The third of the ten ditches of Malebolge, the eighth circle, where different kinds of fraud are punished.
The next ditch. Dante calls it a tomb because each of its sinners is buried in a hole.

The Baptistery of Florence, dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, where Dante and every Florentine child of his time were baptized. He writes of it with love from exile, and in Paradiso 25 he dreams of being crowned as a poet there.

quote: for the baptizers to stand in
note: The old font of the Baptistery, since removed, had round wells let into it. It is still debated whether these were the basins themselves or places where the priests stood, out of the crush of the crowd.

quote: I broke to save someone who was drowning
note: Nothing is known of this incident except what Dante says here. He seems to be answering a charge of sacrilege: he did break part of the font, but to save a life.
A seal on a document proved it genuine. Dante gives his word, as if under seal, that this is what really happened.

The punishment turns the sinners' lives upside down. They set money, a thing of the earth, above the things of Heaven, so they are planted head down in the ground. They pocketed wealth, and the rock pockets them.

quote: The soles of all their feet were aflame
note: A parody of holy things. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down on the apostles' heads as tongues of fire (Acts 2). Here fire plays on the feet of their unworthy successors. The oily surface recalls the holy oil used to anoint priests.
The higher the office that was abused, the hotter the fire. This one was a pope.
The bank between the third ditch and the fourth. Virgil carries Dante down its steep inner side to the floor of the ditch.

In Florence, hired killers were executed by being planted head down in a pit, which was then filled with earth. A condemned man might call the friar back to confess something more, to put off the moment. The picture reverses the usual roles: Dante, a layman, is the confessor, and the sinner is a pope.

context: The soul in the hole can't see who is standing over him and takes Dante for Boniface, arriving to take his place. By this device Dante damns a pope who was still alive in 1300.

quote: The prophecy has lied to me
note: The damned can see the future (Inferno 10). Dante's Italian says "the writing", as if the future were a book. In it this soul has read that Boniface will die in 1303, so in 1300 he is three years early.
The Church, traditionally the bride of Christ, and so in the care of the pope. The fraud is the way Boniface was said to have won her: by talking his predecessor, Celestine V, into resigning in 1294.
The papal mantle. He was pope.

context: He never gives his name, only a pun on it. His family were the Orsini, and orsa is Italian for a she-bear. The "cubs" he advanced are his relatives.

note: The Italian plays on the word for a purse: above he put money in the purse, and here he is put in one himself.

Each hole holds a line of sinners. When a new one arrives, the one on top is pushed down into the cracks of the rock, and the newcomer takes his place with his feet in the fire. This hole is kept for simoniac popes.
The buying or selling of church offices, sacraments or pardons, named after Simon Magus. Medieval church law counted it among the gravest sins a churchman could commit.

quote: longer than he will remain planted
note: Nicholas died in 1280, so he will have been on top for twenty-three years when Boniface arrives in 1303. Boniface will be pushed down in his turn when the next simoniac pope dies in 1314, after about eleven years.

context: A prophecy made after the fact. Clement came "from the west" because he was from Gascony, in the southwest of France.

note: Not the Jason of the Golden Fleece, seen in the last canto. This Jason bought the office of high priest of Jerusalem from King Antiochus IV of Syria and brought pagan customs into the city (2 Maccabees 4).

context: Clement was believed to owe his election to a bargain with Philip, as Jason owed his priesthood to a king.

quote: I answered him in this way
note: A layman lectures a pope. It is one of the boldest speeches in the poem, and Dante marks it by wondering whether he went too far. Its target is not the papacy, which he reveres, but the men who sold it.

context: Every pope claims to be his successor. Dante's point is that Peter paid nothing for his office and charged nothing for anyone else's.

note: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 16:19). The crossed keys are still the emblem of the papacy.
Christ's words when he called Peter from his fishing nets (Matthew 4:19).
The apostle chosen by lot to fill the place of Judas after the betrayal (Acts 1:15–26). No money changed hands.

context: Nicholas worked to reduce Charles's power in Italy. A story current in Dante's time, now doubted, said he took Byzantine gold to back the plot that ended in the Sicilian revolt of 1282. That would be the "ill-gotten money".
As the author of Revelation, where he sees the great whore seated on many waters (Revelation 17).

quote: her who sits upon many waters
note: In Revelation she is a figure of pagan Rome, drunk on the blood of the martyrs. Dante turns the image on the Rome of the popes: a Church that sells herself to kings.

In Revelation the heads and horns belong to the beast the woman rides. Dante gives them to the woman and makes them good: usually read as the seven sacraments (or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit) and the ten commandments, which kept the Church strong while her "husband", the pope, loved virtue.

quote: a god of gold and silver
note: The prophet Hosea's charge against Israel: "of their silver and their gold they have made idols" (Hosea 8:4). It also recalls the golden calf of Exodus 32.

context: Dante blames the gift, not the giver. In his view the Church was meant to be poor, and Constantine's good intention was the start of its corruption.

note: The Donation of Constantine: the grant of Rome and the western empire that the emperor was believed to have made to the pope. The document was an eighth-century forgery, exposed only in the fifteenth century. Dante thought it real, and a disaster.
Sylvester I, pope from 314 to 335, who in legend cured Constantine of leprosy and baptized him.
Grim humor. The only reply the pope can make to Dante's "song" is to kick.
In the next canto Virgil will scold Dante for pitying the damned. Anger at this sin is the right response, and he shows his approval by carrying Dante up in his arms.
